title: Twining
abstract: Hypertext is now commonplace: links and linking structure nearly all of our experiences online. Yet the literary, as opposed to commercial, potential of hypertext has receded. One of the few tools still focused on hypertext as a means for digital storytelling is Twine, a platform for building choice-driven stories without relying heavily on code. In Twining, Anastasia Salter and Stuart Moulthrop lead readers on a journey at once technical, critical, contextual, and personal. The book’s chapters alternate careful, stepwise discussion of adaptable Twine projects, offer commentary on exemplary Twine works, and discuss Twine’s technological and cultural background. Beyond telling the story of Twine and how to make Twine stories, Twining reflects on the ongoing process of making.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Twining (2021), published by Amherst College Press, has been cited 15 times — enough that OpenAlex puts it in the top 10% of works in its field and year. Beyond that, it has been downloaded 2,749 times and is used in teaching.

Full narrative

Twining by Anastasia Salter and Stuart Moulthrop was published by Amherst College Press in 2021. Conceptually, the work connects to Hypertext, Storytelling, Process (computing), Computer science and World Wide Web. The book was recognised: ACLS Open Access Book Prize & Arcadia Open Access Publishing Award finalist (2026) — Literary/Media Studies.

OpenAlex records 15 citations. That places it in the top 10% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2022 with 4 citing works. Notable citing venues include Human-computer interaction series, Humanities and New Review of Hypermedia and Multimedia. The citing works include 8 journal articles and 2 book chapters. They come from 5 countries, led by the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada.

In teaching, it is discussed in 2 recorded lectures. It has been downloaded 2,749 times via OAPEN. It is recorded in 1 library collection. Its subject matter aligns with Quality Education among the Sustainable Development Goals.

The latest English Wikipedia check verified 3 article–work reference matches. These are references or bibliography entries, which may include other editions of the same work; they do not measure readership.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Twining shows strong early scholarly uptake and substantial open-access reach: it has 15 citations, places in the top 10% most-cited works for its field and year, and has recorded 2,749 downloads. The book also appears to have a clear teaching presence, with library holdings and recorded video use, while its open availability through multiple repositories likely supports continued circulation.

Full narrative

Twining is already reading as an influential contribution to hypertext and digital storytelling scholarship. Its 15 OpenAlex citations, combined with a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10%, indicate that the book has moved beyond initial visibility into measurable academic uptake. The citing literature is concentrated in areas closely aligned with the book’s themes, especially digital games and media, interactive narrative, educational games, and hypertext-related computer science, suggesting that the book is being used as a reference point across both humanities and computing-adjacent research.

Usage evidence reinforces that scholarly attention is being matched by broad access. The book has 2,749 downloads in OAPEN metrics, and it is available through multiple open repositories, including OAPEN, DOAB, and Project MUSE. That open circulation matters here because the book’s subject is the contemporary practice of Twine and choice-driven digital storytelling, a topic that sits at the intersection of technical method, literary form, and pedagogy. The record shows that readers are finding and using the work, not just citing it.

The citing landscape also points to pedagogical and applied relevance. Recent citations include work on teaching electronic literature with Twine, digital fiction workshops in academic libraries, and related studies in interactive fiction, archives, and media communication. This pattern suggests that Twining is functioning as a conceptual anchor for educators and researchers working with digital narrative in classroom and workshop settings, particularly in the education sector where most citing activity is located.

The book’s record is quieter in public event data, and that should be read as limited evidence rather than limited effect: the archive does not provide event coverage here. Even so, the combination of citations, downloads, open access availability, and teaching-adjacent use presents a coherent picture of a book with active scholarly and instructional influence. Its alignment with Quality Education further underscores that its impact extends into learning-oriented contexts, where it supports the study and practice of digital storytelling.
